sections.history: Melakadambur lies in the southern reaches of the Kaveri delta, near Kattumannarkoil in Cuddalore district. In the Tevaram hymns of Appar and Sambandar the place is Tirukkadambur, and the temple is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams on the northern bank of the Kaveri. The old village later divided into Melakadambur and Keezhakadambur, so pilgrims take care to ask for the western one. The granite temple seen today is dated by inscriptions to the reign of Kulottunga Chola I, with a record from his forty-third year corresponding to 1113 CE, and it is thought to stand in place of a still earlier brick shrine. Worship has continued here without a break, long past the age of the kings who raised the stone.
sections.architecture: This is a Karakkoil, a temple conceived as a chariot, and one of the very few that survive. The sanctum and its tower are shaped as a processional car, with a pair of horses carved as if drawing it forward on wheels, and the whole superstructure is cut from granite. Panels on the walls show Shiva in his many forms, scenes from the Ramayana and the life of Krishna, and the stories of the Nayanmar saints. Within the enclosure are separate shrines for the goddess Vidyujyothi Nayaki, for Murugan, and for Vinayaka, who is honoured here as Aaravara Vinayaka. The kadamba tree, from which the village takes its name, is the sacred tree of the temple.
sections.legends: Two legends meet in this shrine. In the first, the gods churned the ocean of milk and began to drink the nectar without first worshipping Vinayaka. He took the pot away, and as he carried it through the kadamba forest a single drop fell and became a self-manifested linga. The gods begged his pardon, and Vinayaka returned the pot and bade them worship Shiva here as Amirthakadeswarar, the lord of the nectar. In the second, Aditi, mother of the gods, came daily to worship at this temple, and Indra, unwilling to see her travel so far, turned the temple into a chariot to carry it to his own heaven. Vinayaka pressed down on the car with his foot and halted it, and the left wheel remains sunk in the earth, which is why the temple stays on this ground.
sections.festivals: A rare solar observance is kept on the third, fourth, and fifth days of the Tamil month of Panguni (March to April), when at sunrise, around quarter past six, the rays of the sun are said to fall on the linga for some fifteen minutes and special worship is offered. Maha Shivaratri in Masi, the annabhishekam of Aippasi, Arudra Darshan in Margazhi, Panguni Uthiram, and the monthly Pradosham are all observed. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Come early, while the stone is still cool, and walk around the sanctum slowly to see it as its builders meant it to be seen: a chariot at rest, its horses leaning into their harness. Look for the sunken wheel that the legend remembers, then enter to see Amirthakadeswarar before turning to the goddess Vidyujyothi Nayaki and to Aaravara Vinayaka. The village is small and quiet, set among paddy fields, and few visitors arrive, so the carvings can be studied at leisure. Photographers and students of temple architecture come for the Karakkoil, and devotees come for the nectar-lord, and both leave with the same sense of having found something rare.

visit.timings: Typically open for a short morning session and again in the evening, with a long midday closure; one listing gives about 7:30 to 9:30 in the morning and 5:00 to 8:00 in the evening. Confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards, where the chariot-form sanctum can be photographed from outside, but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Melakadambur is about 7 km from Kattumannarkoil in Cuddalore district and about 34 km from Chidambaram, which has the nearest major railway station. Buses run to the village from Kattumannarkoil and Chidambaram, and a private taxi from either town is the most reliable way to reach it. The nearest major airports are Tiruchirappalli and Chennai, a few hours away by road. Take care not to confuse it with Keezhakadambur, a separate village with its own temple.
